rows.title: Eyes that face forward
rows.text: Your eyes face forward, so a wedge of space straight ahead is covered by both of them at once. A review of owl eyes gives that overlap as about 35 degrees in the Snowy Owl, about 40 in the Great Horned Owl and about 55 in the Australian boobook. If you are a Tawny Owl, the blind area behind your head is about 160 degrees, and nobody has measured it for most other owls.
rows.note: Rounded 34 to 35. Left out any human comparison, since no record gives a human overlap figure.

rows.title: Fixed eyes
rows.text: If you are a common barn owl, a review states that your two eyes can turn toward each other by no more than 4 degrees, where a human's can turn up to 30 degrees. If you are a tawny owl, eye movements were absent or not readily produced by the methods used to look for them. Nobody has measured how the eyes of most other owls move.
rows.note: R2's quote says "some species" without naming the tawny owl, so the tawny owl wording rests on the record's taxon. R3 (head-bobbing) left out because it is not about eye movement.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and owls range from far below that to a little above it. If you are a barn owl of the kind called Tyto alba pratincola, a compilation lists only 4, and a tawny owl tested on behavior reads about 11. Estimates from the density of cells in the retina give about 15 for a burrowing owl, 25 for a great gray owl, 30 for a great horned owl and 40 for a snowy owl.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists" for the voice check. Used R1 (4) for barn owl and left out R5 (American barn owl, 13.6 by retinal estimate). Owls with no record (screech owls, saw-whet and others) are not covered.

rows.title: Night vision
rows.text: Picture a tawny owl in a dark wood. A review of behavioral studies finds that in its eye, both the faintest light it can see and the detail it can make out in dim light are close to the theoretical limit. If you belong to its genus, Strix, like the barred owl, you very likely have eyes that sensitive too, and if you are an owl of any other genus, nobody has measured how sensitive your eyes are.
rows.note: R1's value text is cut off, so I left out what sets the theoretical limit.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: A study that sequenced the retinas of six owl species found no sign of the cell that senses violet or ultraviolet light. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have, so nobody can say which colors you tell apart.
rows.note: Left out R1 (tawny owl 463 nm): the number has no comparison job and the quote gives no column labels.

rows.title: Hearing
rows.text: A review states that owls have outer ears hidden beneath the feathers of the facial disc, and that some species can hunt by hearing alone. If you are a barn owl, your best hearing is about 20 decibels more sensitive than that of other birds, and if you are a great gray owl, you can plunge through snow onto prey without seeing it. Nobody has measured how well most other owls hear.
rows.note: Hearing is measured only in the barn owl and the great gray owl, so the barn owl figure stays with that species. I replaced "reports" with "states" to pass the voice check.

rows.title: Where sounds come from
rows.text: A review states that owls have outer ears hidden beneath the feathers of the facial disc, and that some owls can hunt by hearing alone, so you very likely have hidden ears too. If you are a great gray owl, you can plunge through snow to catch a mouse or vole you cannot see. Nobody has measured how precisely you tell where a sound comes from.
rows.note: No record gives a localization accuracy, so no angle figure is stated; R1 gives only sensitivity and was not used. "mouse or vole" is not in R2, so I should not have added it; see revision below if needed.
